title: Vegetarian Wellington
subtitle: Mushroom, spinach, and chestnut filling wrapped in puff pastry
excerpt: A vegetarian Wellington is a mushroom, spinach, and chestnut filling wrapped tightly in puff pastry and baked until golden. It takes the structure of the beef Wellington: layers of filling inside a pastry case: and replaces the fillet with a robust vegetable and nut filling that slices cleanly and holds its shape.
sourceNotes: A modern vegetarian adaptation of the Beef Wellington format, developed as a Christmas and Sunday centrepiece for vegetarian guests. The chestnut and mushroom filling pattern is widely used in British vegetarian cooking from the 1980s onward.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble the Wellington up to 24 hours ahead and refrigerate, uncooked, on a lined tray. Brush with egg wash just before baking.

content.text: A vegetarian Wellington works on the same principle as the beef version: a filling that can be wrapped, holds its shape when sliced, and gives a dramatic cross-section. The most reliable filling is a combination of mushroom duxelles, cooked spinach, and roasted chestnuts, all dried out well before wrapping. The thing most often done wrong is leaving too much moisture in the filling, which makes the pastry steam rather than bake.

Blitz the mushrooms in a food processor to a coarse paste, or chop very finely by hand. Melt the butter in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook the shallots for 3 minutes, add the garlic and thyme, then add the mushrooms. Cook for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring frequently, until the mixture is almost dry and dark. Season well and tip into a bowl to cool.

Wilt the spinach in the same pan with no added fat, in batches. Squeeze out every drop of water: roll in a clean cloth and wring hard. Chop finely and add to the mushroom mixture. Mix in the chopped chestnuts. Taste and season.
The filling must be completely cool and as dry as possible before wrapping. Spread it on a tray and refrigerate for 20 minutes if needed.

Roll the pastry to a rectangle about 35 x 30 cm. Spread a thin layer of mustard down the centre. Mound the filling in a log shape along the centre, leaving a 5 cm border on each long side and a 3 cm border at each end. Compact the filling as tightly as possible.

Brush the pastry border with beaten egg. Fold the long sides up and over the filling, pressing to seal at the top. Fold and tuck the ends neatly. Turn the whole Wellington over so the seam is underneath and place on a lined baking tray. Brush all over with egg wash. Chill for 30 minutes.

Heat the oven to 210°C fan. Score the top lightly with a knife. Brush again with egg wash. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until deep golden and crisp. Rest for 10 minutes before slicing with a sharp serrated knife.

items.symptom: Pastry is soggy underneath after baking
items.cause: Too much moisture in the filling
items.fix: Squeeze the spinach very hard: it holds far more water than it appears to. Cook the mushrooms until properly dry. Assemble cold, not warm.

items.cause: The filling was not packed tightly enough inside the pastry
items.fix: Use the cling film or a bench scraper to compress the filling into a tight, compact log before wrapping. A loose filling falls apart.

items.symptom: Pastry splits at the seam during baking
items.cause: Seam not sealed firmly enough, or the Wellington was baked directly from room temperature after assembly
items.fix: Press the seam firmly and chill for at least 30 minutes before baking. The cold sets the pastry structure before the heat starts working.

items.cause: The mushrooms were not seasoned at the cooking stage and the overall seasoning was low
items.fix: Season the mushrooms generously during cooking: they can absorb a lot of salt. The chestnuts and spinach both need seasoning too. Taste the cooled filling before assembling.

content.text: The vegetarian Wellington emerged in the 1980s and 1990s as an answer to a common problem: what to serve vegetarian guests at a roast dinner. The format: something in pastry, sliced at the table: gives it the same ceremony as a beef Wellington. It became a regular feature of British Christmas menus. It is now often made for its own sake, not just as a substitute.
